standard_prerequisites: Quasi-coherent modules on algebraic spaces, covers by disjoint unions of affine schemes, and the go-up lemma allowing the statement to be checked after a surjective etale base change
Lazard's theorem that a flat module is a filtered colimit of free modules, and commutation of tensor product with colimits
The limit criterion that a vanishing statement stable under base change holds already at some stage of a filtered colimit of closed subschemes
core_obligations: Replace the space by a surjective etale cover which is a disjoint union of affine schemes, and then reduce the statement to each affine piece, combining the resulting ideals by summing them
Reduce the test morphism to an affine scheme by taking a finite affine open cover of it and replacing it by the disjoint union

In the affine case replace the situation by a map of modules over a ring, use that the target is flat and Lazard's theorem to express each value of the map through a free module on which the value dies after base change, and collect the coefficients of the chosen elements into an ideal of the base ring
Show that the corresponding closed subscheme contains the test morphism and kills the map after base change

In the finite type case with quasi-compact support, write the ideal as a filtered union of finitely generated ideals and use the limit criterion and the finite presentation input to replace it by one of them
proof_roadmap: Reduce to an affine space and an affine test scheme by etale covers and finite affine covers
Build the killing ideal through Lazard's theorem applied value by value
Upgrade to a finitely generated ideal in the finite type case by the limit criterion
difficulty_reason: The counted conclusion is the existence of a closed subscheme through which the test morphism factors and over which the map vanishes at source lines 1566-1575, label lemma-F-zero-somewhat-closed, whose proof occupies source lines 1577-1624. The proof is a genuine computation rather than a reduction: after cutting the space and the test scheme down to affine pieces it replaces the statement by a map of modules over a ring, and since the target module is flat it invokes Lazard's theorem to write each value of the map through a free module on which the value already dies after the given base change, collects the coefficients into an ideal, and checks that this ideal does the job. The finiteness statement is a second argument: the ideal is written as a filtered union of finitely generated ideals and the limit criterion picks one of them, which uses the finite type assumption and quasi-compactness of the support. The counted statement records neither the Lazard step nor the limit argument.
